name: Netflix 2016: two regions, Zuul, EVCache, Hystrix, Open Connect
description: The approximate architecture of Netflix in 2016. Almost all video streaming comes from Open Connect: Netflix puts cache servers in ISP data centers around the world and fills them from the source files in AWS during off-peak hours. Only browsing, sign-in and the API calls before playback go to AWS: in each region, Zuul is the front door for all device requests (routing, authentication, rate limiting), with hundreds of microservices behind it. Most services are stateless and keep state in caches or databases: EVCache (based on memcached) sits in front of Cassandra and other databases and holds viewing history, ratings and recommendations. Dependencies that are not required (for example, recommendations) are wrapped in Hystrix, which returns a default list when they fail. Netflix runs in three AWS regions, and any region can serve any member; Chaos Kong exercises move all traffic of a region to the others. The source says that without cross-region replication, the moved traffic hits cold caches and the many misses overload the databases, so EVCache replicates across regions with Kafka. Sources: https://netflixtechblog.com/caching-for-a-global-netflix-7bcc457012f1 , https://github.com/Netflix/zuul/wiki , https://github.com/Netflix/Hystrix/wiki , https://openconnect.netflix.com/ . The parameters are small values for teaching, not Netflix's real numbers.

nodes.label: Open Connect (caches in ISP data centers)

notes.text: Try it: 1) Run the scenario first: us-east goes down at second 30 for 60 s (Chaos Kong). Video streaming goes through Open Connect and never fails; the problem is the browsing and pre-playback API, where about 27% of requests fail, and the error rate over the run is 9.1%. There are three kinds of failure: DNS needs 10 s to detect that us-east is down, and after that the DNS caches on devices (TTL 60 s) still send part of the requests to the dead region (down, about 18,000); all traffic moves to us-west, the recommendation service is fully busy, and Hystrix's 300 ms timeout and the open breaker make requests fail (about 12,000). 2) Turn on "fallback" on both API→Hystrix connections: when recommendations fail, a default list is returned, the timeout and breaker failures become about 12,000 degraded responses, and the error rate is 5.5%; all remaining failures are requests sent to the dead region. 3) Then change the DNS TTL to 5 s: requests to the dead region drop to about 6,200, and the error rate is 2.8%. But traffic moves to us-west sooner, Zuul and the API queue up, and p99 reaches about 2.8 s. Changing only the TTL without fallback is worse (about 9.9%). 4) Then set the recommendation service in both regions to 4 instances (like Netflix, which keeps enough capacity in each region for all traffic): the error rate is 1.9%, and p99 goes back to about 0.2 s. The remaining failures are from the 10 s before the failure is detected.

Simplified: Netflix runs in three AWS regions; only two are shown here. Hundreds of microservices are combined into one API service and one recommendation service. The cross-region replication of EVCache and Cassandra is not simulated, and each region has its own copy; the thundering herd from caches that go cold when traffic moves cannot be simulated either. A real region evacuation moves traffic slowly with Zuul and DNS together; here there is only DNS failover. The 98% Open Connect hit ratio and all server counts and milliseconds are small values.
